sections.title: Clairaut's Equation
sections.content: A special non-linear differential equation of the form y = px + f(p), where p = dy/dx. The beauty of this equation is its general solution: simply replace 'p' with an arbitrary constant 'c'. General Solution: y = cx + f(c).

sections.title: Singular Solutions
sections.content: A singular solution satisfies the DE but cannot be derived from the general solution by putting a specific value for 'c'. It represents the envelope of the family of curves given by the general solution.

sections.title: Orthogonal Trajectories in Polar Coordinates
sections.content: If the family of curves is in polar form r = f(θ), form the differential equation in r, θ, and dr/dθ. Then replace dr/dθ with -r²(dθ/dr) and integrate to find the orthogonal trajectories.

sections.title: Applications: Growth and Decay
sections.content: Rate of change is proportional to the current amount: dx/dt = kx (growth) or dx/dt = -kx (decay). The solution is always exponential: x(t) = x₀ * e^(kt). Half-life (decay) or Doubling time (growth) is ln(2)/k.

sections.title: Applications: Newton's Law of Cooling
sections.content: The rate of change of temperature of a body is proportional to the difference between its temperature and the ambient temperature (T_s): dT/dt = -k(T - T_s). Solution: T(t) = T_s + (T₀ - T_s)e^(-kt).

sections.title: Complex Substitutions (Polar Conversions)
sections.content: For highly complex DEs involving x² + y², substitute x = r cosθ and y = r sinθ. This implies x² + y² = r² and x dx + y dy = r dr. This transforms complex Cartesian DEs into simpler polar DEs.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
1) Confusing the Singular Solution with the General Solution in Clairaut's equation.
2) Forgetting the r² term when replacing dr/dθ with -r²(dθ/dr) in polar orthogonal trajectories.
3) Using temperatures in Celsius/Fahrenheit when the specific cooling formula requires absolute Kelvin (though for differences, it cancels out, be careful with ratios).

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: Level 3 enters JEE Advanced territory: Clairaut's equation and its singular envelopes, polar orthogonal trajectories, advanced polar substitutions, and real-world exponential applications.

tricks.title: Clairaut's Direct Answer
tricks.explanation: If you see y = x(dy/dx) + f(dy/dx), DO NOT integrate. The general solution is instantly y = cx + f(c).
tricks.example: y = px + a/p → General solution is y = cx + a/c.

tricks.title: Finding Singular Solutions Quickly
tricks.explanation: Take the general solution of Clairaut's equation y = cx + f(c). Treat 'c' as the variable and differentiate the whole equation w.r.t 'c'. Set to 0 to find 'c' in terms of x and y, then substitute back.
tricks.example: y = cx + c². Diff w.r.t c: 0 = x + 2c → c = -x/2. Substitute back: y = x(-x/2) + x²/4 = -x²/4.

tricks.title: Polar Exact Differentials
tricks.explanation: Memorize these conversions: x dx + y dy = r dr. (x dy - y dx) = r² dθ.
tricks.example: If equation is (x dx + y dy) / (x² + y²) = dy/x, it converts to (r dr)/r² = dθ → dr/r = dθ.

tricks.title: Newton's Cooling Approximation
tricks.explanation: If a body cools from T1 to T2 in time 't', and the surrounding temp is Ts, use the average temperature formula for a quick approximation: (T1 - T2)/t = k * [(T1 + T2)/2 - Ts].

tricks.title: Orthogonal Trajectory of y² = 4ax
tricks.explanation: The orthogonal trajectory of a family of parabolas y² = 4ax (where 'a' is a parameter) is an ellipse: x² + y²/2 = C.
tricks.example: Memorizing this specific locus result saves 5 minutes of calculus in MCQ tests.

tricks.title: Mixing Problems Setup
tricks.explanation: For tank mixing problems: dx/dt = (Rate In * Conc In) - (Rate Out * Conc Out), where Conc Out = x(t) / Volume(t).
tricks.example: Sets up the Linear Differential Equation immediately without getting lost in word problem text.
